finding.claim: SSRF via a bypassable host allowlist. The check uses host.endswith("example.com") with no leading dot, so any domain ending in that string passes, e.g. attacker-example.com or evilexample.com. The defined ALLOWED_SUFFIX (".example.com") is never used. An unauthenticated attacker registers such a domain and makes the server fetch an arbitrary URL they control. They can point its DNS at internal IPs such as 169.254.169.254 or 127.0.0.1, and the scheme and port are not restricted. Only len(r.text) is returned, so the impact is mainly blind SSRF: reaching internal services and side-effecting GET requests, plus a response-length oracle.

host.endswith("example.com") — suffix check without a dot boundary; the dot-prefixed ALLOWED_SUFFIX at line 7 is unused
c.get(url) fetches the original attacker-supplied URL

finding.guards_checked: Hostname suffix check at line 13: bypassable with attacker-example.com. No scheme check, no port check, no resolved-IP check against private or loopback ranges, and no authentication on the route. httpx's default follow_redirects=False means redirect-based bypass is not possible, so the finding rests on the suffix bypass and DNS pointing at internal addresses. GET /ping (line 20) uses a constant URL and is SAFE.

verdict.guard_found: Only host.endswith("example.com") at mirror.py:13 (suffix check, no dot boundary); no scheme/port/IP checks, no auth or middleware anywhere in the directory.
